name: steady
_comment: Step 3: the steady-state read baseline.  EVERY read number in this repo,
including today's 1.15x and 1.31x, is a transient: the record cache was
still filling when the measurement ended.  Warmups of 5/20/60 s gave hit
rates of 53.8% / 60.5% / 69.6% on the same workload and build, with
evictions=0 throughout -- so we have never measured what this fork
actually does once the cache stops growing.
Warmup is 900 s for the larger-than-memory arm, and the number to check
FIRST is cached_records.  MEASURED by configs/warmup_sweep.json on
2026-09-16, at the 256 MiB ring A1 restored:
warmup   cached     hit%   evictions
420 s    924532    35.6           0   <- still filling, NOT steady
1800 s   1105020    35.0       73904   <- plateau confirmed
420 s -- what this config used, and what every ltm number before
2026-09-16 was measured at -- never evicted once, i.e. the ring had not
filled and the run was measuring its own warmup.  900 s saturates and 1800 s
confirms the plateau, so 900 is the floor here.
Do NOT read agreement between REPEATS as evidence of steady state: every
repeat is a fresh process warming for the same duration, so two runs that
are both too short agree perfectly.  Only a warmup axis answers it.
And note the fill is driven by OPERATIONS, not wall-clock: at 420 s a build
16% faster cached 17% more records.  If machine speed or build overhead
changes materially, re-check saturation rather than trusting the seconds.
What saturation bought is worth stating plainly: 20% more cached records
moved the hit rate 35.6% -> 35.0%, i.e. nothing.  Under zipf 0.9 over 60M
rows this cache is pinned near 35% across the capacity range we can reach.
Capacity is not the binding constraint on this workload.
Two sizes on purpose.  big/128 MiB never saturates in reasonable time, so
it measures the regime the thesis claims (larger than memory, cache still
an advantage).  v100/16 MiB saturates in seconds, so it measures the regime
where FIFO retention is the binding constraint -- that is where a REF-bit
CLOCK eviction policy would pay, and this tells us by how much.

experiments.name: ltm_steady
_why: Larger than memory: 6.8 GB under a 384 MiB cap, so the OS page
cache cannot stand in for the engine's own.  This is the number
the thesis's point-read claim rests on.

experiments.name: saturated
_warmup_why: 420 s, not the 900 s default: this arm saturates in seconds.  It
evicted ~160k times at 420 s and cached_records reproduced to within
0.06% across three separate campaigns (68260 / 68269 / 68309), so it
is demonstrably at steady state already.  Raising it to 900 would add
an hour to the campaign and change nothing.
_why: A 16 MiB ring against 4M rows cycles within seconds, so this is
the steady state WITH eviction.  Compare the hit rate against
the zipf ideal for the number of records actually cached: the
difference is what FIFO retention costs.
That difference used to be described here as the prize for a
'REF-bit CLOCK policy'.  CLOCK is NOT in the paper or in
cb_copy_on_access_ratio of the ring, 0.0 = FIFO, 1.0 = LRU,
swept in the paper's Figure 14 -- plus a per-record REF bit
consulted ONLY during that copy, to discard cold records.
